# Exact root concavity for two-layer depth and controlled center motion

Let A_0,A_1 be full-dimensional compact convex bodies in R^d, d>=1, placed at integer bases 0 and 1 with their ordinary d-volume measures. Write m_i=|A_i| and m=min(m_0,m_1). Fix a REAL base theta in (0,1), put

    D_theta=(1-theta)A_0+theta A_1,
    p_theta(y)=inf{mu(H): H closed ambient halfspace,
                              (theta,y) in H}.

Then the following is a genuine concavity theorem:

    p_theta((1-t)y_0+t y_1)^(1/d)
       >=(1-t)p_theta(y_0)^(1/d)+t p_theta(y_1)^(1/d)     (1)

for every y_0,y_1 in D_theta and 0<=t<=1. No cap-nonemptiness hypothesis is imposed. The continuous center can move, and every oblique ambient cap is retained.

This is not a Gamma_d lower bound for the maximum of p_theta. The exact crossed rectangles in `candidate 81c79b42fe3af95e` already disprove a 2Gamma_d V endpoint-only bound at theta=1/2.

## 1. Inverse cap thresholds are concave in the volume root

Fix a unit vector u. For each i let

    F_i(s)=|A_i intersect {u.x>=s}|,
    l_i=min_(A_i) u.x,   h_i=max_(A_i) u.x.

F_i is continuous, strictly decreasing on [l_i,h_i], with endpoint values m_i and zero. Strictness follows because every nonempty open slab inside the projection interval meets the interior of the full-dimensional body. Closed supporting sections have zero d-volume.

Define q_i:[0,m_i^(1/d)]->[l_i,h_i] by

    F_i(q_i(r))=r^d,
    q_i(0)=h_i, q_i(m_i^(1/d))=l_i.

The function q_i is continuous, strictly decreasing, and concave. To prove concavity, ordinary cap Brunn--Minkowski gives concavity of F_i(s)^(1/d) for s<=h_i. Indeed the corresponding closed cap bodies satisfy the required Minkowski inclusion; at s=h_i the cap is a NONEMPTY supporting face, not an empty set. For r_0,r_1 and 0<=t<=1, apply this inequality at q_i(r_0),q_i(r_1). It gives

    F_i((1-t)q_i(r_0)+t q_i(r_1))^(1/d)
       >=(1-t)r_0+t r_1.

Since F_i is decreasing, inversion yields q_i((1-t)r_0+t r_1)>=(1-t)q_i(r_0)+t q_i(r_1). The endpoint cases follow directly or by continuity. This is the inverse of a decreasing concave function, with the decreasing sign explicitly retained.

## 2. A fixed allocation set

Set R_*=m^(1/d) and

    Omega={(alpha_0,alpha_1)>=0:
                         alpha_0^d+alpha_1^d=1}.

For 0<=R<=R_* define

    Q_u(R)=min_(alpha in Omega)
        [(1-theta)q_0(R alpha_0)+theta q_1(R alpha_1)].  (2)

The set Omega is compact and, crucially, independent of R. Both arguments R alpha_i stay in the corresponding quantile domains because R<=min_i m_i^(1/d). Each function in the minimum is concave in R, so their pointwise minimum Q_u is concave. It is continuous by compactness and joint continuity.

It is also strictly decreasing. If R_1<R_2, for every alpha at least one alpha_i is positive, and its positive weight (1-theta or theta) multiplies a strictly decreasing quantile. Thus the objective at R_1 strictly exceeds its value at R_2. The difference is continuous on compact Omega and therefore has a positive minimum. Taking minima proves strict decrease. Finally,

    Q_u(0)=(1-theta)h_0+theta h_1=h_(D_theta)(u).        (3)

There is no claim that Q_u as a function of u is a support function.

## 3. Exact inversion, including full and empty endpoint caps

For a real s define the optimized paired cap cost

    K_u(s)=inf_{(1-theta)t_0+theta t_1=s}
                                  [F_0(t_0)+F_1(t_1)]. (4)

Every pair in (4) is exactly the endpoint trace of one finite ambient cap through a point with u.y=s at real base theta. Conversely every such cap gives one pair. Sending the affine tilt to either infinity shows K_u(s)<=m for every s.

For 0<R<R_* the decisive exact equivalence is

    K_u(s)<R^d   iff   s>Q_u(R).                       (5)

If s>Q_u(R), choose an allocation minimizing (2), use thresholds q_i(R alpha_i), and raise BOTH thresholds by s-Q_u(R). Their weighted mean becomes s. Initially the cap volumes sum to R^d. At least one is positive, and neither is full since R^d<m<=m_i. Raising both thresholds strictly decreases at least one positive proper cap, hence the sum becomes strictly smaller than R^d.

Conversely, if K_u(s)<R^d, there are finite thresholds with weighted mean s and cap volumes v_0+v_1<R^d. Both v_i<m_i. Increase these two volumes to v'_i>=v_i with v'_0+v'_1=R^d, increasing at least one strictly. Every v'_i<m_i. Their quantile thresholds q_i((v'_i)^(1/d)) are no larger than the original thresholds: this holds also when an original cap was empty, since its threshold was at least h_i. At least one new threshold is strictly smaller. Their weighted mean is therefore strictly smaller than s. This new allocation is feasible in (2), proving Q_u(R)<s.

In particular K_u(Q_u(R))=R^d: (5) gives the lower bound and the minimizing quantile allocation gives the upper bound. By continuity and monotonicity of Q_u, the complete profile is

    K_u(s)^(1/d)=R_*                    if s<=Q_u(R_*),
                  Q_u^(-1)(s)          if Q_u(R_*)<=s<=Q_u(0),
                  0                    if s>=Q_u(0).   (6)

At s>=Q_u(0), supporting thresholds h_i, raised by a common nonnegative amount, give zero endpoint volume. At the left plateau, (5) for all R<R_* gives K_u(s)>=m, matching K_u(s)<=m. Thus full endpoint saturation is handled by the plateau, not by applying Brunn--Minkowski to an empty cap. The endpoints in (6) agree.

## 4. Concavity on the actual Minkowski section

The function s->K_u(s)^(1/d) is concave on s<=Q_u(0). A direct proof also handles the left plateau. For s_j<=Q_u(0), put r_j=K_u(s_j)^(1/d). Formula (6) gives s_j<=Q_u(r_j). Concavity of Q_u implies

    (1-t)s_0+t s_1
       <=(1-t)Q_u(r_0)+t Q_u(r_1)
       <=Q_u((1-t)r_0+t r_1).

Inversion using (6) proves the required concavity inequality for K_u^(1/d).

For y in D_theta, u.y<=Q_u(0) for every u. Nonvertical caps yield

    p_theta(y)=inf_(|u|=1) K_u(u.y),                    (7)

because each vertical cap takes an entire endpoint fiber and has mass at least m, whereas every K_u<=m. All containing caps can be moved to pass through the point while decreasing mass. Taking the dth root in (7), the pointwise infimum of these concave functions is concave on D_theta. This proves (1).

The function p_theta vanishes on boundary(D_theta) and is positive in its interior. For positivity, an interior point of the Minkowski combination can be represented as a convex combination of two interior endpoint points; a through-point halfspace contains at least one of them, supplying its positive own-depth bound. The representation follows from int(D_theta)=(1-theta)int(A_0)+theta int(A_1), or directly by shrinking both endpoints about interior points and exhausting the Minkowski sum. Boundary vanishing follows from the supporting thresholds in Section 3. No uniqueness of a two-layer deepest point follows from this concavity statement.

## 5. A permitted center motion that retains an endpoint budget

At theta=1/2 write D=(A_0+A_1)/2 and p=p_(1/2). If y_* is any paired center and y_1 is any point of D, then

    p((1-t)y_*+t y_1)
       >=[(1-t)p(y_*)^(1/d)+t p(y_1)^(1/d)]^d
       >=(1-t)^d p(y_*).                               (8)

Now include any actual middle fiber B containing D, with its ordinary own-depth function f_B. At the SAME moved point y_t, every actual cap is bounded below by the sum of the own-middle and paired endpoint minima. Hence

    depth_(A_0,B,A_1)(0,y_t)
       >=[(1-t)f_B(y_*)^(1/d)+t f_B(y_1)^(1/d)]^d
         +[(1-t)p(y_*)^(1/d)+t p(y_1)^(1/d)]^d.         (9)

Ordinary pointwise depth-root concavity proves the first term; (1) proves the second. Vertical caps also obey the sum because f_B<=|B| and p<=m. Formula (9) retains one actual point, every original cap orientation and the actual middle volume. The endpoint y_1 must lie in D; an arbitrary deepest point of B may lie outside D and cannot silently be used in (8)--(9).

This is a new two-layer induction ingredient, not a proof that the maximum in (9) always pays the OC target. More than two layers do not supply the freely variable two-threshold parametrization (4); no extension to an arbitrary many-layer source is inferred.

## 6. Affinely independent source layers

The proof extends exactly to an arbitrary finite simplex of source bases. Let p_1,...,p_N in R^n be affinely independent, let K_i be full-dimensional convex bodies in R^d, and let the measure be the sum of their uniform UNNORMALIZED volume laws on {p_i} times K_i. Fix positive weights lambda_i with sum one and put

    j=sum_i lambda_i p_i,
    D_j=sum_i lambda_i K_i.

Then the dth root of the source depth at (j,y) is concave on D_j.

For a nonzero continuous normal u, affinely independent bases make the endpoint thresholds t_i free subject to the ONE constraint

    sum_i lambda_i t_i=u.y.                             (10)

Indeed values u.y-t_i on p_i have weighted average zero, and affine interpolation realizes them as a base linear form a.(p_i-j). Thus (10) is equivalent to one actual ambient cap through (j,y). Replace Omega in Section 2 by

    Omega_N={alpha_i>=0:sum_i alpha_i^d=1},

and replace (2) by

    Q_u(R)=min_(Omega_N) sum_i lambda_i q_i(R alpha_i),
    0<=R<=min_i |K_i|^(1/d).                            (11)

The allocation set is fixed and compact. The same quantile concavity, uniform strict decrease and exact strict sublevel proof apply, term by term. For N>=2, one can make a selected source full and all others empty while preserving (10), using arbitrarily large finite thresholds; hence the optimized cost is at most the smallest source volume. For N=1 the threshold is fixed and the optimized cost is just the one-body cap cost, already bounded by its full volume. Every purely base-normal cap through j contains at least one whole source, by its positive barycentric representation, so vertical caps cannot lower that value. Equations (6)--(7) and the concavity conclusion follow unchanged.

If the p_i are integers, this is still a theorem about the stated source measure. Its convex hull may have additional integer fibers; those must be retained separately if one applies the statement inside an actual mixed-integer body. The theorem does not erase those fibers or their mass.

## 7. Why dependent source layers are a real boundary

For affinely dependent bases, arbitrary threshold vectors satisfying one barycentric average are not realized by a single ambient cap. They must agree with every affine dependence. Consequently the fixed-allocation formula (11) need not describe the actual cap cost. One cannot simply use one chosen representation and claim equality, nor take a maximum over representations and preserve concavity.

There is already an exact counterexample to the unrestricted extension among actual interval fibers. Use the archived family `candidate 121d9e12ac57cde9`, Sections 1--2, with a=1,b=2:

    K_-=[0,1], K_0=[0,2], K_+=[0,1]

at bases -1,0,1. Its exact ABSOLUTE depth on the entire middle interval is

    f(x)=min{x+min(2x,1),
                  2-x+min(2(1-x)_+,1)}.                (12)

The archived proof minimizes every oblique slope and includes the vertical caps. In particular

    f(3/4)=7/4,  f(1)=1,  f(5/4)=3/4.

Thus f(1)<[f(3/4)+f(5/4)]/2=5/4, disproving root concavity with d=1 for this affinely dependent three-layer source. This is a new consequence of the archived exact profile, not a newly discovered geometric family. The slope of f jumps upward from -3 to -1 at x=1, where f is positive, so every positive power of f also fails local concavity there.

The endpoint-only theorem remains intact: the two outer intervals have Minkowski middle section [0,1], whereas (12) concerns the enlarged actual middle fiber [0,2] and includes its additional source mass. Section 5 states exactly the motion estimate that survives after this enlargement.

The stdlib verifier `../assets/pk-nov6/computations/verify_two_layer_depth_root_concavity.py` checks 1,638 rational quadratic triangle-profile inequalities with unequal endpoint shapes and three real-base weights. It minimizes each piecewise quadratic paired cost exactly, including its full/empty transitions. It also checks the three exact dependent-source values in (12). These are arithmetic diagnostics; the complete general proof is Sections 1--6.

# Exact root concavity for two-layer depth and controlled center motion

**Root concavity of depth on a two-layer Minkowski section**

For full-dimensional A_0,A_1 in R^d at bases 0 and 1 and fixed theta in (0,1), let p_theta(y) be the raw halfspace depth of (theta,y) under the sum of their volume measures. Then p_theta^(1/d) is concave on (1-theta)A_0+theta A_1, positive in its interior and zero at its boundary. Every oblique cap and full/empty endpoint cap is included.

Scope limits: theta is generally a real, noninteger base. No sharp Gamma_d lower bound or uniqueness of the maximizing point follows. Extension in the source uses affinely independent bases, not arbitrary dependencies.

**Dependent source depth need not have any concave positive power**

The explicit dependent interval source in Section 7 of the two-layer note has positive depth value one at the indicated interior point, with one-sided derivatives -3 and -1. Raising depth to any power p>0 leaves an upward derivative jump 2p, so every positive power fails local concavity.

Scope limits: Refutes extension of the affinely independent-source concavity mechanism, not OC. The two-layer theorem itself remains valid.
